Choose an orientation-preserving local crossing chart, whose existence follows from the transversality of the projected branches, in which the over-branch is $(x,0,0)$ oriented by $+\partial_x$, the under-branch is $(0,y,-h)$ for some $h>0$, the viewing normal is $+\partial_z$, and $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$ is the positive projection orientation. Use or radially shrink the chosen product tube near the under-branch to a radius $r$ with $0<r<h$. Choose $d,H>0$ small enough that the chart contains the points below. The source and target points on the upper boundary of the under-tube are $(0,-d,-h+r)$ and $(0,d,-h+r)$; join them by $\beta(y)=(0,y,-h+r)$ for $-d\le y\le d$. Choose a common basepoint in the chosen exterior above the chart and a path $\delta$ in the chosen exterior from it to $(0,0,H)$. The two sides of the triangle in $x=0$ from $(0,0,H)$ to the endpoints of $\beta$, together with $\delta$, give the compatible common-upper-collar access paths to the source and target meridian circles; denote them by $a_s,a_t$. Let $a_o$ be $\delta$ followed by an access arc in the punctured triangle to a small positive meridian circle around the over-strand. The oriented outer boundary of the punctured triangle represents this same based meridian. Base the positive over-meridian by the oriented boundary of this triangle after deleting a small disk about its intersection with the over-strand. Write the resulting based positive meridians as $m_o,m_s,m_t$. The chart, tube, and compatible paths are part of the data. All displayed based loops are in the link or string-link complement group, identified with the group of the chosen compact exterior by radial retraction in the product tubes.

For these compatible accesses,
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o.$$
Equivalently, the crossing relator is $m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}=1$. Reversing the direction of the under-strand does not change this side-based equation.

For arbitrary access paths $a'_e$ to the same chosen meridian circles, let $a_e$ be the compatible access, $c_e=a'_ea_e^{-1}$, and $m'_e=c_em_ec_e^{-1}$, for $e=o,s,t$. The exact relation for the independently based meridians is
$$m'_t=c_tc_o^{-1}(m'_o)^{-1}c_oc_s^{-1}m'_sc_sc_o^{-1}m'_oc_oc_t^{-1}.$$
A common change of base path conjugates all displayed meridians simultaneously.

Assume countable choice.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link, after
inserting a small type-I curl on any component that has no underpassing point.
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the positive meridians of the strands between
successive underpassing points, with the compatible common-upper-collar accesses of the local crossing rule. At a crossing $c$, write $o(c)$ for the
over-strand and $s(c),t(c)$ for the source and target under-sides defined using
the positive in-plane normal to the over-strand. Set
$$r_c=x_{o(c)}^{-1}x_{s(c)}x_{o(c)}x_{t(c)}^{-1}.$$
Then the assignment of each generator to its based positive meridian induces
an isomorphism
$$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_c\ (c\text{ a crossing})\rangle \cong \pi_1(E_L).$$
Any one crossing relator may be omitted without changing the represented
group. The theorem makes no claim that all relators are independent.

Arbitrary independently based positive strand meridians remain recorded: if $g_e$ is the access difference for strand $e$, its actual class is $y_e=g_ex_eg_e^{-1}$ in this reference presentation. This gives their exact group elements without claiming that the independently conjugated $y_e$ themselves freely generate the upper region or give the displayed uncorrected presentation. A common access change conjugates every generator and preserves the displayed presentation map.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

Let $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ be a nonempty labeled oriented link in $S^3$,
let $G=\pi_1(E_L)$, and choose one based positive meridian $m_i\in G$ for each
component. For every integer $q\geq1$, the homomorphism from the free group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$ defined by $x_i\mapsto m_i$ induces a
surjection
$$F_r\longrightarrow G/\Gamma_qG.$$

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Let $F_r$ be the free group and $E$ the Magnus expansion from the preceding
definition, with augmentation ideal $\mathfrak m$. If
$u\in\Gamma_pF_r$ and $v\in\Gamma_qF_r$ for $p,q\ge1$, then
$$
E([u,v])\in 1+\mathfrak m^{p+q}.
$$
Consequently $E(\Gamma_qF_r)\subseteq1+\mathfrak m^q$ for every $q\ge1$.
In particular, reduction of $E$ modulo $\mathfrak m^{d+1}$ factors through
$F_r/\Gamma_{d+1}F_r$ and its coefficients through degree $d$ are independent
of the representative word.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], the validation stage scans a finite diagram. The degree loop runs from $2$ to $d$, each component traversal visits finitely many undercrossings, and each multiplication, inverse, and truncation in $R_d$ involves only finitely many monomials of degree at most $d$. The output stage scans finitely many index sequences and their finitely many proper subsequences and cyclic permutations. Thus every loop is finite and the procedure terminates.

At degree one, every arc meridian on component $j$ maps to $1+X_j$: conjugate meridians have the same abelianization, and the component meridians are the chosen basis in the free source. This is exactly the initialization $Y_a^{(1)}$. If step 1 inserts a curl, the original underpass-free component had one cyclic strand and the new curl cuts it into one interval strand. The supported isotopy transports its initial meridian, paths, and supplied words to that strand; all other strand symbols are transported bijectively. Thus every existing certificate used by the algorithm is interpreted in the post-curl reference system, including the case with no original underpass.

Assume the series $Y_a^{(\ell-1)}$ correctly represent every strand meridian through degree $\ell-1$, and that $Y_s^{(\ell)}$ represents the source meridian through degree $\ell$. At a source-to-target crossing the group relation is $m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o$; at a target-to-source crossing it is $m_s=m_om_tm_o^{-1}$ by [F2]. In a conjugation $Y_o^{-1}Y_sY_o$, replacing the over-series by another series with the same terms through degree $\ell-1$ changes the product only in degree at least $\ell+1$: the degree-$\ell$ discrepancy in $Y_o$ commutes with the constant term $1$ and first meets a positive-degree term of $Y_s$ in degree $\ell+1$. The two update formulas therefore give the correct target meridian through degree $\ell$. Induction over the finite spanning paths and then over $\ell=2,\ldots,d$ proves every assigned strand series is correct through degree $d$.

By [F3], multiplying the ordered over-meridian factors gives the based string-link longitude or the closed-link blackboard parallel with its self-writhe correction. The arc-series just established make $\Lambda_j$ its Magnus expansion through degree $d$.

In the arbitrary-choice branch, evaluating the finite transport words gives their actual compatible-coordinate expansions by step 2.1 and [F5]; when step 1 inserted a curl, these words have already been transported through the explicit old-to-new strand-symbol identification of step 1.2. The formulas of [F3] therefore give the actual selected longitude expansion before changing root variables. The actual root meridian is $g_jx_jg_j^{-1}$, so its series is $1+X_j+R_j$ with $R_j$ of degree at least two. Substitution of two letter systems agreeing through degree $s$ into $R_j$ gives results agreeing through degree $s+1$, since each monomial has at least two letters. Hence the displayed iteration improves the inverse equation by one degree at each pass, starting correctly at degree one. At pass $d$ it solves $Z_j+R_j(Z)=V_j$ exactly in the truncated ring. The same degree argument proves uniqueness, and consequently also the other composition identity. Thus it is the inverse formal change from compatible to actual meridian coordinates. This also agrees with the group-theoretic change on the finite nilpotent quotient: substitution by the conjugates has identity degree-one map and induces an isomorphism on each finite free nilpotent quotient: apply the arbitrary-basing branch of [F4] to the trivial string link, whose compatible endpoint group is $F_r$, with these exact independently conjugated meridians. Its Magnus series satisfies the same unique inverse equations. The corrected-and-substituted series is therefore exactly the longitude expansion in the chosen actual symbols, including independently based endpoints and all supplied relative winding. No full-group free-basis assertion or unrecorded access cancellation is used.

Under the stated axiom branch [A1], for $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\leq d$, [F5] says the coefficient of $X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ depends only on the longitude class in $F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}$ and is independent of the chosen representative. In string-link mode, [F4] identifies that class uniquely via the bottom-end isomorphism. In closed-link mode, [F4] supplies the required component-meridian lift; the procedure uses the based lift determined by its root arcs and traversal. Thus the coefficient read from $\Lambda_j$ is exactly the based coefficient in [F6].

In closed-link mode, each lower coefficient used for $\Delta_I^b$ is computed by the same procedure at its own finite degree; the finite gcd and quotient operation are exactly those in [F6]. Hence the returned indeterminacy and residue candidate are correct for the selected based word-lift data. The theorem asserts no independence of those choices; that is the separate basing theorem.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link with labeled components $K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive, and with
$n\geq1$ crossings and at least one underpassing point on each component. Fix a
smooth height realization $L_D=\{(\gamma(s),\eta(s))\}\subset\mathbb R^2\times[-1,0]$
such that $\eta(s)=-1$ exactly at the $n$ underpassing points and
$\eta(s)>-1$ elsewhere; at each crossing the overpassing point has height
strictly greater than $-1$. Choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$ about the components of $L_D$, and let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior. Put
$$A=(\mathbb R^2\times[-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\},\quad B=(\mathbb R^2\times(-\infty,-1])\cup\{\infty\},\quad \Sigma=(\mathbb R^2\times\{-1\})\cup\{\infty\},$$
and write $X=S^3\setminus L_D$, $A_L=A\cap X$, $B_L=B\cap X$,
and $\Sigma_L=\Sigma\cap X$. Also put
$A_L^\circ=((\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\})\cap X$.
Then $\Sigma_L$ is a path-connected sphere
with $n$ punctures, $A_L\cup B_L=X$, and $A_L\cap B_L=\Sigma_L$. There are
path-connected open sets $U,V\subset X$ such that $X=U\cup V$, $U$ deformation
retracts onto $A_L$, $V$ deformation retracts onto $B_L$, and $U\cap V$
deformation retracts onto $\Sigma_L$. The set $B_L$ is contractible. The small
circles in $\Sigma_L$ around the $n$ punctures normally generate
$\pi_1(\Sigma_L)$, and they still normally generate after any one circle is
omitted. The inclusion $A_L^\circ\hookrightarrow A_L$ is a homotopy
equivalence. Radial retraction in each chosen product tube identifies
$\pi_1(X)$ with the fundamental group of the chosen exterior $E_L$.

Let $X=U\cup V$, where $U$ and $V$ are open path-connected subsets of $X$, let $U\cap V$ be path-connected, and fix $x_0\in U\cap V$. For the inclusion-induced maps in the diagram

$$\pi_1(U,x_0)\longleftarrow\pi_1(U\cap V,x_0)\longrightarrow\pi_1(V,x_0),$$

the group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$, together with the two inclusion-induced homomorphisms, is a pushout ([[def-pushout-of-group-homomorphisms]]). Equivalently, the canonical homomorphism from any pushout $P$ of the displayed diagram to $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ is an isomorphism. No injectivity of either map from the overlap group is assumed.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $i:S\hookrightarrow M$ be a closed smooth embedded submanifold. Then there are an open neighbourhood $\Omega\subseteq\nu(S)$ of the zero section in the quotient normal bundle and a diffeomorphism $\Phi:\Omega\to U$ onto an open neighbourhood $U$ of $i(S)$ in $M$, with $\Phi(0_p)=i(p)$ for every $p\in S$. Thus $S$ has a tubular neighbourhood in $M$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $M$ be a connected smooth $3$-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$
be a nonempty closed connected smooth embedded surface with
$\pi_1(S)=1$. Suppose there is an open neighborhood $N$ of $S$ such that
$N$ is path-connected and simply connected, and $N\setminus S$ has exactly two
path-connected simply connected components $N_-$ and $N_+$. Suppose also that
$M\setminus S$ is path-connected and contains an embedded compact arc
$\nu$ joining $N_-$ to $N_+$, with an open tubular neighborhood $T$ such that
$T\cap N$ consists of exactly two disjoint open $3$-balls, one in each side
component. Then
$$
\pi_1(M)\cong \pi_1(M\setminus S)*\mathbb Z.
$$
The cyclic factor is represented by a loop that joins the two sides of $N$ and
returns between them through $M\setminus S$.

Let $D^2$ be the oriented closed disk and give $C=D^2\times[0,1]$ the product orientation. An $r$-component string link is an ordered family of pairwise disjoint smooth proper embeddings $\tau_i:[0,1]\to C$, for $1\le i\le r$, with fixed distinct endpoints $\tau_i(0)=(p_i,0)$ and $\tau_i(1)=(p_i,1)$ and fixed product collars at the endpoints. Orient each interval from bottom to top. The exterior $X_\tau$ is obtained by removing the relative interiors of chosen pairwise disjoint product tubes around the intervals. The bottom and top punctured disks $P_-$ and $P_+$ are the copies of $D^2$ with the interiors of the endpoint tube disks removed.

Choose a basepoint on the outer boundary of $P_-$, a path in the side boundary of $C$ to the corresponding top basepoint, and basing paths from these points to the component meridians. Each end inclusion, with the chosen connecting path for the top end, induces a based homomorphism $\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$. For each string component choose a parallel path on its tube boundary from the bottom endpoint to the top endpoint, and choose access paths that close it to a based loop using the fixed side connector. The resulting element of $\pi_1(X_\tau)$ is its based string-link longitude; the parallel and access paths are part of the peripheral datum. The positively oriented boundaries of the endpoint tube disks are the designated meridian loops. Stacking two string links means rescaling them into the lower and upper halves of $C$ and identifying their matching endpoint collars; closure joins each top endpoint to the matching bottom endpoint outside $C$ and retains the component labels.

For a nonempty labeled oriented link $L=K_1\cup\cdots\cup K_r$ in the oriented three-sphere, choose pairwise disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, put $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$, and write $T_i=\partial N(K_i)$. A positive meridian $\mu_i$ is the oriented boundary of a normal disk, with the disk orientation fixed by the rule that the oriented tangent of $K_i$ followed by the disk orientation gives the ambient orientation. A degree-one parallel is a simple closed curve on $T_i$ whose projection to $K_i$ has degree $+1$. A based longitude is the class of such a parallel transported to the common basepoint by a specified path. When the positive meridians form a basis of $H_1(E_L;\mathbb Z)$, the self-meridian coordinate of a longitude is its coefficient on $[\mu_i]$. A preferred zero-self-meridian longitude is a chosen degree-one parallel whose self-meridian coordinate is zero. The choice, when it exists, is part of the peripheral datum; this definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. Changing a common basing path conjugates the peripheral group elements simultaneously.

derivations.claim: Let $A_L^\circ=((\mathbb R^2\times(-1,\infty))\cup\{\infty\})\setminus L_D$. By [F1], $\pi_1(A_L^\circ)\cong\pi_1(A_L)$. A small neighborhood $H$ of $\infty$ in $A_L^\circ$ is the open upper half-ball together with its cone vertex $\infty$, disjoint from $L_D$; other points of the level-sphere boundary have been deleted. The open cover $A_L^\circ=M\cup H$ has intersection $H\setminus\{\infty\}$, which is homeomorphic to $(0,1)\times\operatorname{int}(S^2_+)$ and is contractible because the open hemisphere $\operatorname{int}(S^2_+)$ is an open disk. Since $H$ is also contractible, [F2] gives $\pi_1(M)\cong\pi_1(A_L^\circ)$.

Each $D_j$ is the image of the open region $(s,t)\mapsto(\gamma(s),-1+t(\eta(s)+1))$ with $s\in I_j$ and $0<t<1$; this is an embedded open disk. At a projected double point, the underpassing branch has height $-1$ and is absent from $M$, while the overpassing branch has height greater than $-1$. Thus sheets over distinct intervals are disjoint. Each sheet is closed in $M$: its only limit points outside itself lie on the excluded plane $z=-1$ or on the excluded link. Hence it is a proper smooth embedded simply connected surface.

At a fixed vertical line, every point of $Z$ lies above all link points on that line. Since every link height is at most $0$, the straight homotopy $(x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y,(1-t)z+t)$ ($0\le t\le1$) stays above those link points and contracts $Z$ onto the plane $z=1$. This plane is contained in $Z$, so $Z$ is contractible.

For $j=1,\ldots,n$, put $M_j=M\setminus\bigcup_{k>j}D_k$. Then $M_0=Z$ and $M_j=M_{j-1}\cup D_j$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the smooth normal-bundle structure used in the
framing clause. For a knot component $K$, its normal bundle is the fibrewise
quotient $\nu K=TS^3|_K/TK$, and a normal section is a smooth section of this
bundle.

Let $D$ be a regular oriented link diagram in a projection plane $P$ of an
oriented $3$-sphere, after moving the link off the point at infinity. Fix the
unit viewing normal $n$ pointing toward the viewer. Orient $P$ by the rule that
an ordered basis $(u,v)$ of $P$ is positive exactly when $(n,u,v)$ is a positive
basis of the ambient $3$-space. At a crossing $c$, let $v_{\rm over}$ and
$v_{\rm under}$ be the nonzero projected tangent vectors following the
orientations of the overpassing and underpassing strands. Define
$$\operatorname{sgn}(c):=\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})\in\{+1,-1\}.$$
Reversing the orientation of $P$ reverses every crossing sign.

This convention makes the positive geometric Artin half twist positive. In
the braid chart $(x,y,t)$ with ambient orientation $(x,y,t)$, view along $+y$;
the induced positive orientation of the $(x,t)$ projection plane is the ordered
basis $(\partial_t,\partial_x)$. For the positive half twist, label $i$ moves
from $x=-h$ to $x=h$ below the midpoint, while label $i+1$ moves from $x=h$ to
$x=-h$ above it, with $h>0$. Thus the over and under projected tangent vectors
in coordinates $(t,x)$ are $(1,-2h)$ and $(1,2h)$, whose determinant is
$4h>0$.

The **writhe** of $D$ is
$$\operatorname{wr}(D):=\sum_{c\text{ a crossing of }D}\operatorname{sgn}(c).$$
For a link component $K_i$, its **self-writhe**
$\operatorname{wr}_i(D)$ is the sum over crossings whose two branches belong to
$K_i$; the total writhe also includes all mixed crossings between distinct
components.

The **blackboard framing** of a component of $D$ is the homotopy class of the
normal section represented by the positive quarter-turn in $P$ of the projected
oriented tangent. The projection is an immersion, so this vector never
vanishes; it is perpendicular to the projected tangent, hence also to the
spatial tangent, and therefore represents a nonzero normal section of the
component in the ambient $3$-sphere.

```tikz
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8,>=stealth]
  \draw[->] (-1,0) -- (1,0) node[right] {$v_{\rm over}$};
  \draw[->] (0,-1) -- (0,1) node[above] {$v_{\rm under}$};
  \node[above left] at (0,0) {$+1$};
\end{tikzpicture}
```

In the displayed local chart, the over tangent is the positive horizontal
vector and the under tangent is the positive vertical vector, so the determinant
is $+1$. This figure illustrates the determinant rule only; no proof below
depends on a picture.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

Assume AC. Let $\tau$ be an $r$-component based string link with $r\geq1$,
exterior $X_\tau$, and endpoint punctured disks $P_-,P_+$. Use compatible jointly transported stem accesses for the positive
endpoint meridians to identify $\pi_1(P_-)$ and $\pi_1(P_+)$ with the free
group $F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, and let
$\iota_\pm:\pi_1(P_\pm)\to\pi_1(X_\tau)$ be the based end homomorphisms,
including the chosen top connecting path. For every integer $q\geq1$, each
induced map
$$\iota_{\pm,q}:F_r/\Gamma_qF_r\longrightarrow \pi_1(X_\tau)/\Gamma_q\pi_1(X_\tau)$$
is an isomorphism. Their composite
$\iota_{-,q}^{-1}\iota_{+,q}$ is the based nilpotent comparison of the labeled
top and bottom peripheral systems.

Arbitrary independently based positive endpoint meridians are retained as well: the map from the free symbol group $F_r$ sending $x_i$ to that chosen meridian need not identify the full fundamental group, but its composites with the end maps still induce the displayed isomorphisms on every finite lower-central quotient. Their inverse/composite is the comparison for those exact choices, and the conjugating access differences are part of the data.

Assume AC for the string-link quotient branch. Use the closed-link residue
definition one finite maximum index length at a time, so its based word-lift
data are finite.

Let $\tau$ be a based $r$-component string link with bottom meridian symbol group
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$, exterior group $G=\pi_1(X_\tau)$, and
based string-link longitudes $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r$. With compatible stem accesses this free group identifies the full endpoint fundamental group. For arbitrary independently based meridians, use instead its meridian map on each finite nilpotent quotient, which is still an isomorphism by the end-identification theorem; no full-group free-basis assertion is made. Longitudes retain their specified parallel and access data. For a multi-index
$I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$ with $k\geq1$ and each index in $\{1,\ldots,r\}$,
let $w_{j,k}\in F_r/\Gamma_{k+1}F_r$ be the unique class whose image under
the bottom-end nilpotent isomorphism is the class of $\lambda_j$ in
$G/\Gamma_{k+1}G$. Define the integer coefficient
$$\mu_\tau(I)=[X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}]\,E(w_{j,k})\in\mathbb Z,$$
where the bracket means the coefficient of that word in the finite Magnus
expansion through degree $k$. The commutator-degree lemma makes this coefficient
independent of the representative of $w_{j,k}$.

For a closed labeled link $L$, choose a common basing and its preferred
zero-self-meridian longitudes. For every component $j$ and every finite
$q\geq2$, choose a lift $w_{j,q}\in F_r/\Gamma_qF_r$ of the class of its
longitude in $G/\Gamma_qG$, where $G=\pi_1(E_L)$ and $F_r$ is free on the
component meridian symbols. Such lifts exist because those meridians generate
every finite nilpotent quotient. For $I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, define the based
coefficient $\mu_L^b(I)$ by taking the coefficient of
$X_{i_1}\cdots X_{i_k}$ in $E(w_{j,k+1})$ through degree $k$. Let
$\Delta_I^b$ be the nonnegative greatest common divisor of the finite set of
all $\mu_L^b(J)$ for sequences $J$ of lengths from $2$ to $|I|-1$ that occur
as subsequences of cyclic permutations of $I$. The gcd of an empty set is $0$.
Define the based residue candidate
$$\bar\mu_L^b(I):=\mu_L^b(I)\pmod{\Delta_I^b}\in \mathbb Z/\Delta_I^b\mathbb Z,$$
with $\mathbb Z/0\mathbb Z=\mathbb Z$. Independence of the basing and word
lifts is not part of this definition; it is a separate theorem. A based
Borromean example with $I=(1,2,3)$ uses this convention.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

The input is a finite regular oriented link diagram together with its declared
components. If it does not have exactly two components, return
`invalid-input`. For a two-component diagram $D$, initialize $s:=0$ and make
one pass over its finite crossing list. At each crossing whose branches lie on
different components, add
$$\operatorname{sgn}\det_P(v_{\rm over},v_{\rm under})$$
to $s$, where the determinant is taken in the oriented projection plane; ignore
self-crossings. Return $s/2$. The even-sum lemma establishes that this output is
an integer and is the diagram's linking number.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. On every finite regular oriented diagram
with exactly two components, the crossing-scan algorithm halts after one
iteration per crossing and returns the integer half-sum of the mixed crossing
signs. On an input with any other number of components it returns
`invalid-input` after the finite component-count check.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume countable choice.

Let $D$ be a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled link, after
inserting a small type-I curl on any component that has no underpassing point.
Let $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ be the positive meridians of the strands between
successive underpassing points, with the compatible common-upper-collar accesses of the local crossing rule. At a crossing $c$, write $o(c)$ for the
over-strand and $s(c),t(c)$ for the source and target under-sides defined using
the positive in-plane normal to the over-strand. Set
$$r_c=x_{o(c)}^{-1}x_{s(c)}x_{o(c)}x_{t(c)}^{-1}.$$
Then the assignment of each generator to its based positive meridian induces
an isomorphism
$$\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\mid r_c\ (c\text{ a crossing})\rangle \cong \pi_1(E_L).$$
Any one crossing relator may be omitted without changing the represented
group. The theorem makes no claim that all relators are independent.

Arbitrary independently based positive strand meridians remain recorded: if $g_e$ is the access difference for strand $e$, its actual class is $y_e=g_ex_eg_e^{-1}$ in this reference presentation. This gives their exact group elements without claiming that the independently conjugated $y_e$ themselves freely generate the upper region or give the displayed uncorrected presentation. A common access change conjugates every generator and preserves the displayed presentation map.

Let $D$ be a finite oriented diagram of a nonempty labeled closed link or string link, with a chosen smooth realization and pairwise-disjoint product tubes. Choose a crossing whose two projected branches meet transversely and for which no other branch meets a sufficiently small neighborhood, and let $o$ be the over-strand. Orient the projection plane by the rule that $(v_1,v_2)$ is positive exactly when $(n,v_1,v_2)$ is positive in the ambient three-space, where $n$ is the viewing normal. Let $n_o$ be the positive in-plane normal characterized by $(v_o,n_o)$ being positive. The source side $s$ is the side from which $n_o$ points, and the target side $t$ is the side toward which it points.

Choose an orientation-preserving local crossing chart, whose existence follows from the transversality of the projected branches, in which the over-branch is $(x,0,0)$ oriented by $+\partial_x$, the under-branch is $(0,y,-h)$ for some $h>0$, the viewing normal is $+\partial_z$, and $(\partial_x,\partial_y)$ is the positive projection orientation. Use or radially shrink the chosen product tube near the under-branch to a radius $r$ with $0<r<h$. Choose $d,H>0$ small enough that the chart contains the points below. The source and target points on the upper boundary of the under-tube are $(0,-d,-h+r)$ and $(0,d,-h+r)$; join them by $\beta(y)=(0,y,-h+r)$ for $-d\le y\le d$. Choose a common basepoint in the chosen exterior above the chart and a path $\delta$ in the chosen exterior from it to $(0,0,H)$. The two sides of the triangle in $x=0$ from $(0,0,H)$ to the endpoints of $\beta$, together with $\delta$, give the compatible common-upper-collar access paths to the source and target meridian circles; denote them by $a_s,a_t$. Let $a_o$ be $\delta$ followed by an access arc in the punctured triangle to a small positive meridian circle around the over-strand. The oriented outer boundary of the punctured triangle represents this same based meridian. Base the positive over-meridian by the oriented boundary of this triangle after deleting a small disk about its intersection with the over-strand. Write the resulting based positive meridians as $m_o,m_s,m_t$. The chart, tube, and compatible paths are part of the data. All displayed based loops are in the link or string-link complement group, identified with the group of the chosen compact exterior by radial retraction in the product tubes.

For these compatible accesses,
$$m_t=m_o^{-1}m_sm_o.$$
Equivalently, the crossing relator is $m_o^{-1}m_sm_om_t^{-1}=1$. Reversing the direction of the under-strand does not change this side-based equation.

For arbitrary access paths $a'_e$ to the same chosen meridian circles, let $a_e$ be the compatible access, $c_e=a'_ea_e^{-1}$, and $m'_e=c_em_ec_e^{-1}$, for $e=o,s,t$. The exact relation for the independently based meridians is
$$m'_t=c_tc_o^{-1}(m'_o)^{-1}c_oc_s^{-1}m'_sc_sc_o^{-1}m'_oc_oc_t^{-1}.$$
A common change of base path conjugates all displayed meridians simultaneously.

Let the diagram be either a based regular string-link
diagram in $D^2\times[0,1]$ or a finite regular oriented diagram of a nonempty
labeled closed link. In either mode write its labeled components as
$K_1,\ldots,K_r$, where $r$ is positive. In closed-link mode, choose pairwise-disjoint closed product tubes $N(K_i)$, let $E_L=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\bigl(\bigcup_iN(K_i)\bigr)$ be their compact exterior, and choose the positive meridian circles on their boundaries; these tube and peripheral choices are part of the input. In string-link mode, choose the product-tube parallel to
be the blackboard push-off determined by the projected tangent, carried
through the fixed endpoint collars. Choose one initial strand on each component. Let $x_e$ denote the compatible based positive meridian of strand $e$, and let $x_j$ be the meridian on the chosen initial strand of component $K_j$. For the literal diagram word below first use compatible common-upper-collar accesses to all positive strand meridians and the induced endpoint accesses for the parallel; a common change of the complement base path is allowed. Arbitrary independent access paths and other degree-one parallels remain allowed, with their exact correction formula specified below. Traverse component $K_j$ in its orientation
(from bottom to top for a string link and once around for a closed link). At
each undercrossing $c$ of $K_j$, let $o(c)$ be the over-strand, and set
$\epsilon_c=+1$ if the traversal goes from the source side to the target side
of the over-strand's positive in-plane normal, and $\epsilon_c=-1$ if it goes
from target to source. If the undercrossings in traversal order are
$c_1,\ldots,c_s$, define
$$W_j(D)=x_{o(c_1)}^{\epsilon_{c_1}}\cdots x_{o(c_s)}^{\epsilon_{c_s}}.$$
For a string link, this word represents its based longitude. For a closed
link, it represents the blackboard parallel in $\pi_1(E_L)$. The preferred
zero-self-meridian longitude in the closed-link case is represented by
$$\lambda_j(D)=x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}W_j(D),$$
where $x_j$ is the initial meridian on $K_j$ and $\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$ is
the sum of crossing signs at self-crossings of $K_j$.

For the arbitrary-choice branch, write $a_e$ for the compatible access to the chosen meridian circle of strand $e$ and $a_e'$ for the actual access, after recording any endpoint-on-the-circle connectors. Put $g_e=a_e'a_e^{-1}$ and $y_e=g_e x_e g_e^{-1}$. The compatible word expressed in these actual meridians is
$$\widehat W_j=\prod_{c\text{ in traversal order}}g_{o(c)}^{-1}y_{o(c)}^{\epsilon_c}g_{o(c)}=W_j.$$
Let $a_0,a_1$ be the compatible accesses to the initial and terminal points of the blackboard parallel, with the fixed side connector included in $a_1$ for a string link. For a closed component these are the same access. Record actual accesses $a_0',a_1'$ and put $h_0=a_0'a_0^{-1}$, $h_1=a_1'a_1^{-1}$. For a chosen parallel $\beta'$ with the same endpoint coordinates as the blackboard parallel $\beta$, let $k\in\mathbb Z$ be its relative meridian winding, so $\beta'\simeq\mu_0^k\beta$ on the tube. A closed degree-one parallel is included; then $h_0=h_1=h$. Its actual based class is exactly
$$h_0x_j^k\widehat W_jh_1^{-1}.$$
For a closed component its self-meridian coordinate is $k+\operatorname{wr}_j(D)$, and its preferred zero-self-meridian correction is
$$h\,x_j^{-\operatorname{wr}_j(D)}\widehat W_j\,h^{-1}.$$
Thus arbitrary changes are retained as explicit transport and winding factors; independent access choices are not silently assumed to give the literal uncorrected product in the $y_e$.

For every group $G$ and $i,j\ge1$, $[\gamma_i(G),\gamma_j(G)]\le\gamma_{i+j}(G)$. The rule $(x\gamma_{i+1},y\gamma_{j+1})\mapsto[x,y]\gamma_{i+j+1}$ is a well-defined biadditive map between the abelian lower-central factors.

For any group $G$, define its lower-central series by $\Gamma_1G=G$ and
$\Gamma_{q+1}G=[G,\Gamma_qG]$, where $[G,H]$ is the subgroup generated by
$ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$ for $g\in G$ and $h\in H$. For $r\ge1$, let
$F_r=\langle x_1,\ldots,x_r\rangle$ be the free group on the formal meridian
symbols $x_i$, with the free-group convention of its stated generators.

Let $\mathcal A_r=\mathbb Z\langle\!\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle\!\rangle$
be the ring of formal integer sums $\sum_w a_wX_w$ over all finite words $w$
in the letters $X_i$, with multiplication given by concatenation of words.
This is the degree-complete ring for the word-length filtration; a series with
invertible constant coefficient is a unit, with inverse determined recursively
degree by degree.
Filter it by total degree (word length), and let $\mathfrak m$ be the ideal of
series with zero constant term.
The Magnus expansion is the group homomorphism
$$E:F_r\longrightarrow \mathbb Z\langle\!\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle\!\rangle^\times, \qquad E(x_i)=1+X_i.$$
It sends $x_i^{-1}$ to $(1+X_i)^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^kX_i^k$. For an
integer $d\ge0$, calculations through degree $d$ use the truncated ring
$R_d=\mathbb Z\langle X_1,\ldots,X_r\rangle/\mathfrak m^{d+1}$. As a
$\mathbb Z$-module it has the finite monomial basis of words of length at most
$d$. In $R_d$, the inverse of $1+A$ for $A\in\mathfrak m$ is the finite sum
$1-A+A^2-\cdots+(-A)^d$.

For a based string link, $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ may be used as formal symbols
corresponding to the positive bottom-end meridians. No freeness or
lower-central quotient isomorphism is asserted here; those properties require
separate proofs.

derivations.claim: Cut the traversal of component $i$ just before its initial arc. For every other arc $a$ of that component let $v_a$ be the signed product of over-arc symbols encountered before $a$; for the initial arc set $v_a=1$. The nonclosing relations in [F1] successively say $a=v_a^{-1}x_iv_a$. The final relation on that component is $x_i=W_i^{-1}x_iW_i$, with $W_i$ the full traversal product. This rewriting follows by induction along the traversal and does not treat an over-arc as an already eliminated free generator.

Define words in $F$ simultaneously by $P_a^{(1)}=x_i$ and $P_a^{(s+1)}=v_a(P^{(s)})^{-1}x_iv_a(P^{(s)})$, retaining $P_a^{(s)}=x_i$ at each initial arc. Substitution in a finite word preserves congruence modulo a normal subgroup. If the substituends change modulo $\Gamma_s$, the conjugate of a weight-one generator changes only modulo $\Gamma_{s+1}$, because $[F,\Gamma_s]\subseteq\Gamma_{s+1}$ by [F3]. Consequently $P_a^{(s+1)}\equiv P_a^{(s)}\pmod{\Gamma_{s+1}F}$: the case $s=1$ is equality in the abelianization, and this observation proves the induction. In $G$, the true arc meridian equals $P_a^{(s)}$ modulo $\Gamma_{s+1}G$, by the same induction starting from conjugate meridians in the abelianization.

Put $P_a=P_a^{(q-1)}$, $W_i=W_i(P^{(q-1)})$ and $l_{i,q}=x_i^{-\operatorname{wr}_i}W_i$. Step 2.1 and [F2] show that these are longitude lifts in $G/\Gamma_qG$. The relation $[x_i,l_{i,q}]=1$ is equivalent to $[x_i,W_i]=1$. Let $H$ be the quotient of $F$ by these relations and $\Gamma_qF$. Its root-meridian map to $G/\Gamma_qG$ is defined because the true meridian and its true peripheral parallel commute on the boundary torus. Every arc meridian is the image of $P_a$, so this map is onto.

Conversely assign every Wirtinger arc the image of $P_a$ in $H$. If an undercrossing does not close its component, its conjugation equation follows from the consecutive partial traversal products evaluated at $P^{(q-1)}$: those products give $P^{(q)}$, and $P^{(q)}\equiv P^{(q-1)}$ modulo $\Gamma_q$ by step 2.1. At the closing crossing the same argument leaves exactly $[x_i,W_i]=1$, imposed in $H$. Thus all crossing relations hold. By [F1] this gives $G\to H$, and it factors through $G/\Gamma_qG$ because $H$ is a quotient of $F/\Gamma_qF$. The two maps are inverse: they fix every root generator of $H$, and step 2.1 says their composite fixes every arc generator of $G/\Gamma_qG$. This proves the displayed presentation and the kernel assertion.

For a fixed finite maximum degree, the iterates in step 2.1 stabilize in every lower quotient; applying the same observation to the finite word $W_i$ proves coherence of $l_{i,q}$. Finally, forming a further quotient adds the prescribed relations to the kernel. Surjectivity in step 3.1 means every conjugating element of $G/\Gamma_qG$ has a lift in $F$, so the added relations are exactly $[u^{-1}x_iu,v^{-1}x_iv]$ for words $u,v\in F$. Their entire normal closure is meant; the argument does not assert this infinite family is finite.
